links.outcome: Sensitivity and fairness metrics across ethnicity, race, and sex subgroups for AD progression models
links.effect: Sensitivity was lower for Hispanic participants; true positive rate difference ranged from 20.9% (5.5%) for RNN to 27.8% (9.8%) for SVM in MCI and 24.1% (5.4%) to 48.2% (17.3%) in AD. Sex fairness generally satisfied.
links.quote: Sensitivity for predicting progression to MCI and AD was lower for Hispanic participants compared with non-Hispanic participants; the difference (SD) in true positive rate ranged from 20.9% (5.5%) for the RNN model to 27.8% (9.8%) for the SVM model in MCI and 24.1% (5.4%) for the RNN model to 48.2% (17.3%) for the LR model in AD.

links.outcome: Model performance for underrepresented racial and ethnic groups in a cohort that was 92.4% White
links.effect: Sensitivity was lower for Black and Asian participants vs non-Hispanic White participants; AD true positive rate difference for Black vs White was 14.5% (LR), 12.3% (SVM), 28.4% (RNN). Models were accurate in aggregate but failed fairness metrics.
links.quote: Sensitivity was similarly lower for Black and Asian participants compared with non-Hispanic White participants; for example, the difference (SD) in AD true positive rate was 14.5% (51.6%) in the LR model, 12.3% (35.1%) in the SVM model, and 28.4% (16.8%) in the RNN model for Black vs White participants, and the difference (SD) in MCI true positive rate was 25.6% (13.1%) in the LR model, 24.3% (13.1%) in the SVM model, and 6.8% (18.7%) in the RNN model for Asian vs White participants.

screen.reason: Empirical study auditing algorithmic fairness across demographic subgroups for AD progression models; it identifies performance disparities but does not test an organizational deployment practice or mitigation safeguard.
